n: Hoshea becomes Israel’s last king and reigns nine years (about 732–722 BC).
He did evil, though not as badly as earlier kings. Even so, the kingdom’s accumulated sin had reached its end.
Shalmaneser V of Assyria comes against him, and Hoshea submits as a vassal, paying tribute.

f.g: Shalmaneser V, king of Assyria 727–722 BC.
tribute.

n: Hoshea secretly seeks help from Egypt and stops paying tribute. Assyria treats this as rebellion and imprisons him. Isaiah and Hosea had warned against trusting Egypt.

f.g: an uncertain figure, perhaps an Egyptian ruler or the city of Sais.

f.w: sent messengers to So king of Egypt

n: Assyria overruns the land and besieges Samaria for three years.

Samaria falls in 722 BC. The Israelites are deported to distant regions of Assyria and Media. These are the “lost ten tribes.” Latter-day Saint scripture teaches they will be gathered again, and that the keys for their gathering were restored.

f.r: Articles of Faith 1:10; D&C 110:11; 3 Nephi 17:4; 2 Nephi 29:13

f.g: a region in northern Mesopotamia.

f.w: Habor by the river of Gozan
f.g: the Habur River, a tributary of the Euphrates.

n: The narrator now pauses for a sermon explaining why it happened: Israel sinned against the God who freed them from Egypt and revered other gods.

f.g: revered, worshiped.

n: They adopted the customs of the Canaanites whom the Lord had driven out, along with practices their own kings introduced.

f.g: the religious customs of the pagan nations.

n: They secretly did wrong and built shrines everywhere, from the smallest watchtower to the largest walled city.

f.w: from the tower of the watchmen to the fenced city
f.g: an idiom meaning everywhere, from tiny outposts to big cities.

n: They set up sacred pillars and Asherah poles on every hill and under every leafy tree.

f.g: sacred stone pillars and Asherah poles.

n: They burned incense at these shrines as the expelled nations had.
They served idols in direct violation of the Lord’s explicit command.

f.w: Ye shall not do this thing

n: The Lord sent prophet after prophet calling Israel and Judah to repent. Exile came only after long patience and repeated warnings.

f.g: prophets who see visions.

n: They refused to listen and “hardened their necks” like a stubborn ox resisting the yoke—just like their ancestors.

f.g: were stubborn, unwilling to submit.

n: They rejected God’s covenant and followed worthless idols—and became worthless themselves. We become like what we worship.

f.g: pursued emptiness and became empty.

n: They made the two golden calves, an Asherah pole, worshiped the stars, and served Baal.

f.g: the sun, moon, and stars worshiped as gods.

n: They sacrificed children, practiced divination and sorcery, and “sold themselves” to evil.

f.g: fortune-telling and magic spells.

n: So the Lord, in great anger, removed Israel from His presence; only Judah remained.
An aside: Judah was not innocent either, and followed Israel’s ways—a warning of its own coming exile.
The Lord let all Israel’s descendants be afflicted and plundered until they were cast out.

f.g: plunderers, raiders.

n: It began when Israel broke from David’s house and made Jeroboam king, who drove them away from the Lord.

f.w: he rent Israel from the house of David

n: Israel never departed from Jeroboam’s sins.
Finally, as the prophets warned, the Lord removed Israel from its land into Assyria, where they remained “unto this day.”

f.w: as he had said by all his servants the prophets

n: Assyria resettled foreign peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, Hamath, and elsewhere in Samaria’s towns—a standard Assyrian policy to break national identity.

f.g: a city in Babylonia; later Jews sometimes called Samaritans ‘Cutheans.’
a city of uncertain location, perhaps in Syria.

n: The newcomers didn’t worship the Lord, and lions began killing some of them—a sign that the land belonged to the Lord.
They told the Assyrian king they didn’t know the customs of “the god of the land,” thinking of the Lord as a local deity who needed to be appeased.

f.w: the manner of the God of the land
f.g: the proper rituals for the local god.

n: The king orders an exiled Israelite priest sent back to teach them.
The priest settles at Bethel—the old center of calf worship—and teaches them to fear the Lord.
But each group also made its own gods and placed them in the hilltop shrines.
Each people brought its own deities: Succoth-benoth, Nergal, Ashima—gods of Babylon, Cuthah, and Hamath.

f.g: a Mesopotamian god of the underworld and plague.

n: Others worshiped Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites even burned their children to their gods.

f.g: gods of Sepharvaim; names possibly linked to ‘melech,’ king.

n: They worshiped the Lord, but also appointed priests from all sorts of people for the shrines.
They feared the Lord yet served their own gods. This mixed religion is the background of the later Samaritans, with whom Jews in Jesus’s day had deep tensions.

f.w: They feared the LORD, and served their own gods

n: To this day, the narrator says, they do not truly fear the Lord or keep His law given to Jacob’s descendants.
The Lord had made a covenant with Israel: worship no other gods.

f.w: Ye shall not fear other gods

n: Worship the Lord alone, who brought you out of Egypt with a “stretched out arm”—a picture of mighty, saving power.
Obey His written law forever, and fear no other gods.
Don’t forget the covenant.
Fear the Lord, and He will deliver you from your enemies—the promise Israel forfeited.
But they would not listen; they kept their old ways.
Generation after generation, these peoples mixed the Lord’s worship with idols. The chapter ends on a sober note about divided loyalty—the very sin Elijah once called “halting between two opinions.”

f.w: both their children, and their children's children
